I. For days, Foryst, my cat, seems to have something caught in his throat. I bring him to the vet. “It might be a
twig,” I say. “Or a pebble.” “What's the cat's name?” she asks. “Foryst,” I say. “Forest,” I say again, “but with a
y where the e should go.” The vet is quiet. “How old is Foryst?” she asks. “Thirteen,” I say. She looks in his
mouth. “It hurts when he swallows,” I say. Foryst is still. The vet sees nothing. She listens to his heart, his
lungs. She hears nothing. It suddenly makes no sense to me that she is a human. Why isn’t she a wolf with great
big eyes and great big ears that are all the better to see him with? To hear him with? “I recommend blood work,”
she says.
I put my face in Foryst's fur. “Please tell me what's wrong.” He is silent. There is something in his throat. A
word or a dead leaf. I am sure of it.
The vet wants blood work. She wants the cold, definitive clink of numbers. I want Foryst to talk so he can tell
me what hurts. I want him to cough up a dry spooked O and be suddenly healed. I want him to tell me the
future. I call my mother. “There's something stuck in Foryst’s throat.” “Of course there's something stuck in
Foryst's throat,” she says. “Why wouldn't there be something stuck in his throat? There's something stuck in all
of our throats.” She hangs up. I swallow once. I swallow twice.
When we get home, I open Foryst’s mouth and shine a flashlight down his throat. Something shines back, like a
diamond in a cave. His teeth are hieroglyphs. I want to jot them down so I can read what's inside him. I want to
reach all the way in, but he snaps his mouth shut and growls.
I tell my husband there is something stuck in Foryst's throat. “What?” he says. He lifts his left headphone from
his ear. “There is something stuck in Foryst's throat.” My husband is always wearing headphones. I say
everything twice.

“Good night, Pinocchio,” says the ghost in “The Talking Cricket.” “May heaven protect you from morning dew
and murderers.” Animals in fairy tales are feral poets. Their words are overgrown and have the scent of
soothsayer and pelt. When an animal speaks it’s often to spill the guts of the fairy tale. To leak the plot and
indict the antagonist. To clear up the past or tell the future. Animals are tattlers and whistleblowers.

II. When the German banking giant Wirecard collapsed in June 2020 amid a roaring fraud scandal, public
opinion was shocked. The company, praised as the country’s innovative answer to the fintech industry of Silicon
Valley, had been widely seen as a ‘German miracle’ following recovery from the 2008 financial crisis. Its
bankruptcy involved a massive state prosecution that sent shockwaves through world markets. To the
astonishment of German and international observers, Wirecard executives were found to be involved in all
manner of deception: direct falsification of accounts, fake cash-flows, re-routing of payments through non-
existing shell companies, ghost subsidiaries. While forging profits, they had obscured a mammoth debt of €3.5
billion.
This, of course, is not an unfamiliar tale. The explosive growth of finance as a percentage of the ‘real’ economy
in recent decades has been matched by an equally dazzling scale of financial fraud, from the Enron scandal to
Bernie Madoff's pyramid scheme (the largest recorded fraud in world history) in the 2000s, to more recent
scams in cryptocurrency markets such as FTX. Denizens of finance both system insiders (Madoff was a former
chairman of the Nasdaq exchange) and ‘maverick’ outsiders (Sam Bankman-Fried of FTX had been seen as a
challenger of mainstream banking elites) have displayed a unique capacity for alchemy: whipping up distorted


realities in which false truth and true fact become indistinguishable. Their plotting is often aided by regulatory
bodies, rating agencies and consultancies that firm up such distorted realities through either action or inaction.
A recent Netflix documentary follows the Financial Times reporter Dan McCrum in his quest to reveal
Wirecard’s own big con. The ‘aha’ moment comes when McCrum and his FT colleagues show up at the
Singapore address of one of the company’s supposed subsidiaries only to find an unassuming farmhouse.
Behind Wirecard’s opaque structure lay simply nothing: no accounts, no offices, no cash. Much of the bank’s
alleged business had been conjured out of thin air. Evocatively subtitled ‘a fight for the truth’, McCrum's
bestselling book Money Men (2022), on which the Netflix show is based, offers an animated account not only of
Wirecard’s fraudsters, but also of their victims those led to believe the company bosses and their outlandish
myths of stratospheric growth, despite ominous clouds of deceit hovering over.
What made a fake story so readily believable by so many? How is it possible that a DAX 30-listed bank (with
the backing of Germany's former chancellor, Angela Merkel, herself) transpired to be a giant Ponzi scheme?

norm-but-a-reflection-of-it

III. We are accustomed to categorizing research as either theoretical, empirical, or a blend of both. However,
there exists a third, less recognized form of study: independent thinking. This form often intertwines with the
other two, albeit subtly. Independent thinking is crucial in research, especially when uncertainties arise around
theoretical and empirical bases. Researchers must reflect on and possibly revise their initial assumptions. This
process, integral to research, often occurs in discussions with colleagues or at seminars, without predefined
starting points.
This form of thinking, although a fundamental part of research, is seldom highlighted in published scientific
articles. These publications don't fully depict the entire research process, focusing instead on the final results.
The informal, yet significant, conversations and reflections that occur during research are typically omitted from
these publications.
The difficulty in recognizing this third form of research lies in our preconceived notions of scientific work,
which are often based on the polished appearance of completed studies. This "facade conception" of research
obscures the actual, often messy, process behind it. This misconception can be particularly challenging for new
PhD students, who might feel inadequate when their research experience doesn't align with the seamless
progression depicted in published articles. Researchers, when seeking funding or ethics approval, are often
compelled to present their projects as if they have already proceeded without any hitches, further perpetuating
this facade.
This blog post itself serves as an example of the third form of research. It encourages us to reconsider our
assumptions and recognize our entanglement in them. Philosophical studies, in particular, often focus on self-
examination of these assumptions. They help us realize that our questions are not just about external phenomena
but also about our own perspectives.
The post suggests reading two publications on embryo donation for stem cell research to illustrate different
research approaches. One is empirical, involving interviews with individuals who underwent infertility
treatment, while the other is a philosophical analysis of concerns about exploitation in embryo donation. The
empirical study provides a basis for ethical and legal discussions, while the philosophical study aims to open up
more thoughtful debates by examining our conceptual entanglements.


The relevance of empirical studies is clear, as they produce results that can be directly applied to debates.
However, philosophical studies, though they may not yield concrete findings, are crucial for understanding and
re-examining our mental starting points. They act like keys, unlocking our awareness of the assumptions we are
bound to.
Both empirical and philosophical studies serve as different types of keys, each contributing uniquely to more
open and thoughtful debates. Empirical studies offer concrete findings for discussion, while philosophical
studies provide the tools for self-reflection and a deeper understanding of the underlying assumptions in
debates.

IV. Roman wakes early. He sloughs off his sleeping bag and swims in the dark to the lab window. Where are
we, where are we? Where on earth. It's night and there’s land. Into view edges a giant city nebula among
reddish-rust-nothing; no, two cities, Johannesburg and Pretoria locked together like a binary star. Just beyond
the hoop of the atmosphere is the sun, and in the next minute it will clear the horizon and flood the earth, and
dawn will come and go in a matter of seconds before daylight is everywhere at once. Central and East Africa
suddenly bright and hot.
Today is his four hundredth and thirty-fourth day in space, a tally arrived at over three different missions. He
keeps close count. Of this mission it's day eighty-eight. In a single nine-month mission there are in total roughly
five hundred and forty hours of morning exercise. Five hundred morning and afternoon meetings with the
American, European and Russian crews on the ground. Four thousand three hundred and twenty sunrises, four
thousand three hundred and twenty sunsets. Almost one hundred and eight million miles travelled. Thirty-six
Tuesdays, for all that, this being one. Five hundred and forty times of having to swallow toothpaste. Thirty-six
changes of T-shirt, a hundred and thirty-five changes of underwear (a fresh set of underwear every day is a
storage luxury that can’t be afforded), fifty-four clean pairs of socks. Auroras, hurricanes, storms their numbers
unknown but their occurrence certain. Nine full cycles, of course, of the moon, their silver companion moving
placidly through its phases while the days go awry. But all the same the moon seen several times a day and
sometimes in strange distortion.
To his tally kept on a piece of paper in his crew quarters, Roman will add the eighty-eighth line. Not to wish the
time away but to try to tether it to something countable. Otherwise the centre drifts. Space shreds time to pieces.
They were told this in training: keep a tally each day when you wake, tell yourself this is the morning of a new
day. Be clear with yourself on this matter. This is the morning of a new day.
And so it is, but in this new day they'll circle the earth sixteen times. They'll see sixteen sunrises and sixteen
sunsets, sixteen days and sixteen nights. Roman clasps the handrail by the window to steady himself; the
southern hemisphere stars are fleeting away. You're bound to Coordinated Universal Time, ground crews tell
them. Be clear with yourself on this matter, always clear. Look often at your watch to anchor your mind, tell
yourself when you wake up: this is the morning of a new day.

questions.stimulus:
LEGAL REASONING

I. Article 22 of the Indian Constitution outlines several rights available to an accused in the case of arrest and
detention. It mandates the duty to inform the accused of the grounds of arrest and to consult a lawyer of choice.
Additionally, it requires the police officer to present the person arrested before a magistrate within twenty-four
hours, ensuring that the individual cannot be detained beyond this period without proper judicial authority.
Under Article 22(1) and Section 41D of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC), an accused person has the
right to be consulted and defended by a legal practitioner of their choice. This right is crucial, especially during
interrogation, although it does not extend throughout the entire interrogation process.
The concept of free legal aid is integral to ensuring justice for all, particularly for those who lack the economic
means to engage in legal proceedings. Article 39A of the Constitution, under the Directive Principles of State
Policy, emphasizes the state's duty to ensure justice is accessible to all citizens, thereby mandating the provision
of free legal aid. This is aimed at creating an equitable justice system where economic constraints do not hinder
access to legal recourse.
Section 54(1) of the CrPC grants the accused the right to a full-body medical examination. This examination
can be crucial in providing evidence that may either disprove the commission of an offence by the accused or
implicate someone else. However, this right is subject to the magistrate's discretion, especially if it is perceived
as a tactic to delay proceedings.
The Constitution provides a framework for the protection of individuals against arbitrary arrest and detention.
Article 22 specifically addresses these concerns, ensuring that the rights of the accused are safeguarded during
the legal process. This includes the right to be informed of the grounds of arrest, the right to legal
representation, and the right to be presented before a magistrate within a specified timeframe.
An arrested individual must be informed of the reasons for their arrest. This is a fundamental right that ensures
transparency and fairness in the legal process. Additionally, the right to legal representation is critical in
safeguarding the interests of the accused, allowing them access to legal counsel to defend their case effectively.
The provisions related to arrest and detention reflect the overarching principles of justice and fairness embedded
in the Indian legal system. These provisions aim to balance the state's power to detain individuals for legal
transgressions with the fundamental rights of individuals, ensuring that the process of arrest and detention is not
abused and is conducted in a manner that respects the dignity and rights of the accused.

https://blog.ipleaders.in/arrest-of-a-person/#Protection_against_arrest_and_detention

II. In a recent Supreme Court ruling, it was determined that a Hindu couple had not legally married despite
holding a marriage certificate, as their marriage was registered under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA)
before performing the necessary wedding rituals. This decision emphasizes the requirement for fulfilling
specific ceremonial rituals to validate a marriage under the HMA, notably those outlined in Sections 7 and 5.
Section 5 of the HMA outlines the conditions for a Hindu marriage, mandating that certain conditions be met
for a marriage to be considered valid. These conditions include the requirement for neither party to have a
spouse living at the time of marriage, both parties to be of sound mind and capable of giving valid consent,
neither party suffering from mental disorders that would render them unfit for marriage and procreation, and
that the bride and groom should not fall within degrees of prohibited relationship unless custom permits.
The distinction between marriage registration and solemnization is crucial under the HMA. Solemnization
refers to the actual marriage ceremonies required by religious practices, which are essential for a marriage to be
recognized as valid under personal laws. In contrast, registration is a formal act of record-keeping that typically
follows the solemnization of the marriage. Under the Special Marriage Act, 1954 (SMA), a civil or "registered"
marriage occurs where the marriage is solemnized without traditional rituals in a registrar's office, and the
registration itself validates the marriage.
For Hindus and some Christian communities in India, marriage is considered a sacrament, necessitating specific
religious ceremonies for a valid union. Conversely, Islamic marriages are based on contractual principles,

requiring mutual consent and witnesses but not ceremonial rites. The nikahnama in Islamic traditions formalizes
the union and is generally recognized even without additional state registration.
Several states, including Karnataka and Delhi, mandate the registration of marriages, highlighting its
importance for legal recognition and administrative purposes. This registration is vital in contexts requiring
proof of marital status, such as applications for spousal visas or inheritance claims.

rituals are observed. While a marriage certificate under the SMA is conclusive evidence of marriage, under the
HMA, the certificate alone is insufficient without the completion of specified rituals, per Sections 5 and 7.

spouse living at the time of marriage, both parties to be of sound mind and capable of giving valid consent,
neither party suffering from mental disorders that would render them unfit for marriage and procreation, and
that the bride and groom should not fall within degrees of prohibited relationship unless custom permits.
The distinction between marriage registration and solemnization is crucial under the HMA. Solemnization
refers to the actual marriage ceremonies required by religious practices, which are essential for a marriage to be
recognized as valid under personal laws. In contrast, registration is a formal act of record-keeping that typically
follows the solemnization of the marriage. Under the Special Marriage Act, 1954 (SMA), a civil or "registered"
marriage occurs where the marriage is solemnized without traditional rituals in a registrar's office, and the
registration itself validates the marriage.

III. The doctrine of "Volenti Non Fit Injuria" plays a critical role. This Latin maxim, translating to "no injury is

bearing inherent risks are precluded from seeking damages for any resulting injury. This principle rests on the
idea that consenting adults are aware of the risks involved and, thus, cannot hold others liable if harm occurs
during such activities.

and certain contractual agreements. In each instance, the person engaged has acknowledged and accepted the
potential for harm, negating their ability to claim compensation later.

obtained through deceptive means such as fraud, coercion, or misrepresentation, rendering the consent invalid.

negligence exceeding what was consented to.
In sports, for example, players assume the normal risks associated with the game but do not consent to conduct
that is outside the rules and could cause unexpected harm. Similarly, patients undergoing surgery give informed
consent only for the risks disclosed to them prior to the operation, not for medical negligence or errors beyond
those risks.

an injury as a result of him doing an act which he knows is likely to cause harm to him but it is an act to rescue
someone, then this defence will not apply and the defendant will be held liable. Therefore, they can seek redress
for injuries sustained during the rescue.

IV. The Tenth Schedule of the Constitution, commonly known as the anti-defection law, lays down the
circumstances in which a member of a legislature incurs disqualification on the ground of defection. A member
elected on the ticket of a political party is liable to be disqualified if the member voluntarily gives up the
membership of that political party or votes, or abstains from voting, contrary to any direction issued by the
political party without prior permission, unless such action is condoned by the political party within fifteen
days. The expression "voluntarily giving up membership" is not confined to formal resignation and may be
inferred from the conduct of the member. An independently elected member incurs disqualification upon joining
any political party after the election, while a nominated member incurs disqualification if the member joins a
political party after the expiry of six months from the date of taking a seat in the House. Any question relating to
disqualification under the Tenth Schedule is decided by the Speaker or the Chairman of the House, whose
decision remains subject to judicial review.

The Constitution recognises only one exception to disqualification on the ground of defection, namely a valid
merger under Paragraph 4 of the Tenth Schedule. A member shall not be disqualified if the original political
party merges with another political party and the member acts in accordance with such merger. A member who
does not accept a valid merger is also protected from disqualification and is entitled to continue functioning as a
separate group within the House. However, constitutional protection is available only when the merger satisfies
all the conditions prescribed under Paragraph 4.
For the purposes of the Tenth Schedule, the "original political party" and the "legislature party" are distinct legal
entities. The original political party refers to the parent political organisation, whereas the legislature party
consists only of the members of that political party in a particular House. The legislature party derives its
existence and authority from the original political party and cannot function independently in matters
concerning merger. Consequently, the decision to merge must originate from the original political party. A
legislature party cannot independently initiate, declare, or create a merger with another political party, and any
such attempt does not satisfy the constitutional requirements governing mergers.

Paragraph 4(2) provides that a merger shall be deemed to have taken place only if not less than two-thirds of the
members of the legislature party concerned have agreed to such merger. The requirement of a two-thirds
majority is mandatory but is not, by itself, sufficient to constitute a valid merger. Such approval acquires legal
effect only after the original political party has resolved to merge with another political party. Therefore, a valid
merger requires the coexistence of two conditions: a merger of the original political party and the approval of
not less than two-thirds of the members of the corresponding legislature party. Failure to satisfy either condition

renders the constitutional exception inapplicable and attracts the ordinary provisions relating to disqualification
under the anti-defection law.

The constitutional position regarding mergers was strengthened by the Constitution (Ninety-first Amendment)
Act, 2003, which omitted the earlier provision recognising splits by one-third of the members of a legislature
party. Following the amendment, the Constitution recognises only mergers supported by not less than two-thirds
of the members of the legislature party, thereby preventing legislators from circumventing the anti-defection
law through smaller breakaway groups.
Judicial interpretation has consistently affirmed the primacy of the original political party under the Tenth
Schedule. In Ravi S. Naik v. Union of India (1994), the Supreme Court held that voluntary relinquishment of
party membership may be inferred from the conduct of a member and does not require a formal resignation. In
Rajendra Singh Rana v. Swami Prasad Maurya (2007), the Court rejected the "two hats theory" and held that
legislators cannot simultaneously claim an independent constitutional identity separate from the original
political party. More recently, in Subhash Desai v. Principal Secretary, Governor of Maharashtra (2023), the
Supreme Court reaffirmed that a legislature party cannot function independently of the original political party in
matters relating to party leadership, organisational authority, or constitutional recognition. The constitutional
scheme, therefore, recognises the original political party as the primary legal entity under the Tenth Schedule,
while the legislature party functions only as its legislative manifestation. Accordingly, protection from
disqualification on the ground of merger is available only upon strict compliance with the constitutional
requirements prescribed under Paragraph 4.

antidefection-law-531690

V. The Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971, as amended in 2021, regulates the conditions under which
pregnancies may be lawfully terminated in India. The Act recognises the reproductive autonomy of women


while prescribing statutory safeguards based upon the stage of pregnancy and the opinion of qualified medical
professionals. As a general rule, a pregnancy may be terminated up to twenty weeks of gestation, provided the
conditions prescribed under the Act are fulfilled and the opinion of one Registered Medical Practitioner is
obtained. For pregnancies between twenty and twenty-four weeks, termination is permissible only for specified
categories of women, including survivors of rape, sexual assault or incest, minors, women whose marital status
changes due to widowhood or divorce during pregnancy, women with physical disabilities recognised under the
Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, mentally ill women including women with mental retardation,
women carrying foetuses suffering from substantial abnormalities likely to be incompatible with life or likely to
result in serious physical or mental disability, and women whose pregnancies occur in humanitarian, disaster or
emergency situations declared by the Government. Termination during this period requires the opinion of not
less than two Registered Medical Practitioners.

The Act imposes stricter conditions once the pregnancy exceeds twenty-four weeks. Termination beyond this
stage is ordinarily prohibited and is permissible only where it is immediately necessary to save the life of the
pregnant woman or where substantial foetal abnormalities are diagnosed in accordance with the statutory
procedure. In cases involving substantial foetal abnormalities after twenty-four weeks, the opinion of the State-
level Medical Board is mandatory. The Act further permits termination of pregnancy on the ground of failure of
any contraceptive method or device, and this ground is available equally to both married and unmarried women.
Thus, while the Act recognises reproductive choice, it subjects such choice to different procedural requirements
depending upon the duration of pregnancy.

The Act also prescribes the places where pregnancy may be lawfully terminated. No termination may be carried
out except in a hospital established or maintained by the Government or at a place specifically approved for the
purposes of the Act by the Government or by a duly constituted District Level Committee. Such Committee is
required to consist of not less than three and not more than five members, with the Chief Medical Officer or
District Health Officer serving as its Chairperson. To ensure confidentiality, Section 5A prohibits a Registered
Medical Practitioner from disclosing the identity or other particulars of a woman whose pregnancy has been
terminated under the Act, except where disclosure is authorised by law. The Act also grants protection to
Registered Medical Practitioners acting in good faith by providing that no civil or criminal proceedings shall lie
against them for any act done or intended to be done in accordance with the Act.

The constitutional validity and operation of the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act have repeatedly come
before constitutional courts. The Supreme Court has observed that the statutory scheme permits termination of
pregnancies beyond twenty-four weeks where substantial foetal abnormalities exist but does not ordinarily
extend similar protection to pregnancies resulting from rape or incest involving minor girls. The Court has
therefore indicated that the legislative framework may require reconsideration to remove the statutory time limit
in cases involving pregnancies of minor rape victims. The issue highlights the interaction between statutory
restrictions and constitutional guarantees of dignity, bodily autonomy and reproductive choice.

Indian constitutional jurisprudence has consistently recognised that a woman's decision whether to continue or
terminate a pregnancy forms part of the right to life and personal liberty guaranteed under Article 21 of the
Constitution. The constitutional protection extends to decisional autonomy, bodily integrity, privacy and the
freedom to determine whether to enter motherhood. Judicial decisions have emphasised that compelling a
woman to continue a pregnancy arising from rape may infringe her dignity and personal liberty by forcing her


to endure continuing physical and psychological trauma. Constitutional courts have therefore interpreted the
Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act in a manner that seeks to balance legislative safeguards with the
fundamental rights of women while ensuring that the statutory requirements governing gestational limits,
medical opinions, approved medical facilities and confidentiality are strictly complied with.

inherently non-transferable, which includes exceptions such as spes successionis (the chance of an heir
succeeding), easements, right of re-entry, interests restricted to personal enjoyment, and the mere right to sue,
among others. For instance, rights that are purely personal or attached to a future maintenance cannot be
transferred. Also, stipends such as military pensions and political pensions are specified as non-transferable
under this section.

separate from the property it concerns, and stipends or pensions, which are personal to the receiver and thus
non-transferable. The prohibition against transferring a mere right to sue underscores the personal nature of

forbidden by law or involve or imply injury to another person or property, ensuring that property transactions
adhere to legal and ethical standards.

questions.stimulus:
IV. Though every leader has a vision, they realise that “has” is not a static term. Maybe “lives with” is more
accurate, since any starter-vision can evolve. It's subject to experience. So, of course, a leader must evolve along
with their vision. How else can they accommodate it? Over time, there's a give and take. Pursuing a vision is an
organic process where you're also redesigning yourself. Does this sound a little New Age? It's not. Just think
about it.
Any vision that we see for ourselves as it slowly, even painfully comes into focus must sync up with how we
work on ourselves to achieve it. Along the way, we can’t expect total clarity as to who we may become. We may
even ask fundamental questions about whether we are up to the task and, even more fundamentally, whether
what we are trying to achieve is right for us.
In other words, questions will arise as to who we are and who we want to be, which only we can answer. No one
else can do our introspection for us. No one else has our imagination. So, my point is that setting out to make a
vision a reality requires that we understand what motivates us, what really makes us tick.
At the very least, in becoming a leader we should be confident that that's what we really want. It's one thing to
have an abstract idea and another to integrate that idea with our lives. Are we willing to sacrifice, and
experience the demands on our time that are required if we commit to such an effort? Can we put up with the
displacement of what used to be our priorities? Can we brush off comments by people who sigh, “I don’t know
you anymore you’re so obsessed”? In effect, when we start living our vision, we must be able to live with
ourselves (though we may not have anticipated the challenges that that might entail).
Of course, we project our vision outwards, onto the world. But living with a vision draws us back towards
ourselves in an exercise of getting to know who we are and feeling comfortable with that. If we're not
comfortable with ourselves, then it will be hard to maintain a vision, much less work towards making it a
reality. If you display some misgivings towards yourself, it's unlikely that other people will be willing to follow
your lead. They may wonder, for example, “If that person is so uncomfortable with what they think, why should
I be any less so?” If you pick up on their hesitancy, you may become even less sure of yourself, creating a
vision-killer vicious circle.
Source: https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/resilience/202312/as-your-vision-of-leadership-evolves-so-
does-your-life

IV. Though every leader has a vision, they realise that “has” is not a static term. Maybe “lives with” is more
accurate, since any starter-vision can evolve. It's subject to experience. So, of course, a leader must evolve along
with their vision. How else can they accommodate it? Over time, there's a give and take. Pursuing a vision is an
organic process where you're also redesigning yourself. Does this sound a little New Age? It's not. Just think
about it.
Any vision that we see for ourselves as it slowly, even painfully comes into focus must sync up with how we
work on ourselves to achieve it. Along the way, we can’t expect total clarity as to who we may become. We may
even ask fundamental questions about whether we are up to the task and, even more fundamentally, whether
what we are trying to achieve is right for us.
In other words, questions will arise as to who we are and who we want to be, which only we can answer. No one
else can do our introspection for us. No one else has our imagination. So, my point is that setting out to make a
vision a reality requires that we understand what motivates us, what really makes us tick.
At the very least, in becoming a leader we should be confident that that's what we really want. It's one thing to
have an abstract idea and another to integrate that idea with our lives. Are we willing to sacrifice, and
experience the demands on our time that are required if we commit to such an effort? Can we put up with the
displacement of what used to be our priorities? Can we brush off comments by people who sigh, “I don’t know
you anymore you’re so obsessed”? In effect, when we start living our vision, we must be able to live with
ourselves (though we may not have anticipated the challenges that that might entail).
Of course, we project our vision outwards, onto the world. But living with a vision draws us back towards
ourselves in an exercise of getting to know who we are and feeling comfortable with that. If we're not
comfortable with ourselves, then it will be hard to maintain a vision, much less work towards making it a
reality. If you display some misgivings towards yourself, it's unlikely that other people will be willing to follow
your lead. They may wonder, for example, “If that person is so uncomfortable with what they think, why should
I be any less so?” If you pick up on their hesitancy, you may become even less sure of yourself, creating a
vision-killer vicious circle.
